<section class="route-brief" id="essentials-overview" aria-labelledby="essentials-overview-title"><h2 id="essentials-overview-title">Start with Essentials</h2>
<p>Start here if you want a first pass through the economics behind a finance decision. Imagine a manager asking why a price changed, what a payment is worth, or whether the firm can still pay on time. Each lesson gives you a small decision you can work through before reading the answer.</p><ol><li><strong>Read the market.</strong> Use prices and quantities as evidence. Check what else could explain what you observe.</li><li><strong>Value the payment.</strong> Put cash flows on the same date and ask which state of the world they arrive in.</li><li><strong>Ask who knows what.</strong> Work out who accepts an offer or sends an order when each side knows something different.</li><li><strong>Stress-test the decision.</strong> Trace a shock through cash, purchasing power, interest expense, and the exchange rate.</li></ol>
<p><a class="primary" href="chapters/market-prices.html?route=essentials">Start the 12-lesson route →</a> <a href="#essentials-takeaways">Jump to takeaways</a></p></section><details class="map-route" id="essentials" data-route-name="The essentials route"><summary><span>Explore the essentials roadmap</span><small>12 lessons</small></summary><h3>Read a market</h3><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="market-prices" href="chapters/market-prices.html?route=essentials">What can a price move tell us?</a><small>A share price rises after an earnings release. Decide which explanation you could defend in a morning note.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="demand-elasticity" href="chapters/demand-elasticity.html?route=essentials">Should the firm raise its price?</a><small>Use a subscription business to see when the same price increase helps revenue and when it hurts.</small></li></ol><h3>Value a payment</h3><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="project-appraisal" href="chapters/project-appraisal.html?route=essentials">Is the project worth funding?</a><small>A project pays more next year than it costs today. Find the financing rate at which the decision reverses.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="risk-insurance" href="chapters/risk-insurance.html?route=essentials">What is full insurance worth?</a><small>Compare the expected loss with the largest premium a household would pay to remove it.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="state-prices" href="chapters/state-prices.html?route=essentials">Why is a recession payoff worth more?</a><small>Two claims have the same average payoff. Recover their prices by building portfolios that reproduce their payments.</small></li></ol><h3>Work with private information</h3><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="adverse-selection" href="chapters/adverse-selection.html?route=essentials">Who accepts the offer?</a><small>A buyer who raises an offer may change the quality of what comes to market. Work out which sellers accept and what their cars are worth.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="dealer-pricing" href="chapters/dealer-pricing.html?route=essentials">Quote the next trade</a><small>A dealer sees a buy order but cannot see who placed it. Use the direction of trade to update the asset value and quote again.</small></li></ol><h3>Stress-test a balance sheet</h3><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="bank-liquidity" href="chapters/bank-liquidity.html?route=essentials">Can the bank meet withdrawals?</a><small>Use a small balance sheet to find the withdrawal that exhausts equity and the larger withdrawal that exhausts cash.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="real-returns" href="chapters/real-returns.html?route=essentials">Did purchasing power rise?</a><small>Read a price index, deflate a sales forecast, and calculate what a nominal investment can actually buy.</small></li></ol><h3>Trace a macro shock</h3><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="business-cycle-shocks" href="chapters/business-cycle-shocks.html?route=essentials">Why did shipments fall?</a><small>Compare the operating evidence behind equal falls in shipments and decide which constraint the firm should address.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="policy-transmission" href="chapters/policy-transmission.html?route=essentials">Can the borrower cover its interest?</a><small>Trace a policy change through a floating-rate loan and distinguish a financing shock from a change in operating earnings.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="hong-kong-exchange-rate" href="chapters/hong-kong-exchange-rate.html?route=essentials">What does the currency link protect?</a><small>Compare the exchange cost of a US-dollar invoice with the Hong Kong dollar interest bill needed to finance it.</small></li></ol><section class="route-takeaways" id="essentials-takeaways" aria-labelledby="essentials-takeaways-title">
<h3 id="essentials-takeaways-title">Essentials route takeaways</h3><ul><li>A price move can have several explanations. Say what evidence would distinguish them.</li><li>The value of a payment depends on its timing and on when you need it most.</li><li>People change their choices as prices and terms change. Recheck who trades and what cash is available on the due date.</li></ul>
<h4>Put it together</h4><p>A Hong Kong importer faces both a weaker HK dollar and higher loan rates. Its customers may also cut orders. What belongs in a short note to the treasurer?</p><details><summary>Read a worked response</summary><p>Separate invoice translation, loan interest, and operating cash flow. In the lesson’s stress example, the invoice costs HK$50,000 more and loan interest adds HK$40,000. Fixing the exchange rate on the invoice leaves the interest cost outstanding. Check order cancellations and available cash before deciding whether the firm should also fix its borrowing rate or arrange a buffer.</p></details>
<p><a href="#essentials-overview">Back to the overview</a></p></section></details><h2 id="professional-routes">Choose a professional route</h2><p>Choose the work you want to practice. Each route gives you a starting question, an ordered set of lessons, and a final decision that uses several of them.</p><div class="route-grid"><details class="map-route" id="investment" data-route-name="Investment analysis"><summary><span>Investment analysis</span><em>What changes the value of a payment, a portfolio, or a long-lived business?</em><small>8 lessons</small></summary><section class="route-brief" id="investment-overview" aria-labelledby="investment-overview-title"><h3 id="investment-overview-title">How this route fits together</h3>
<p>Start with the question an investor asks before committing money. What cash will this investment pay, when will we receive it, and which risks would we still hold? The route starts with a single payment and ends with a valuation you can defend when assumptions change.</p><ol><li><strong>Value cash flows.</strong> Use project appraisal, insurance, and state prices to compare payments across dates and states.</li><li><strong>Choose exposures.</strong> Use portfolio choice and the market-risk benchmark to decide what risk you are taking and how much return you require.</li><li><strong>Challenge the valuation.</strong> Check whether trading behavior, reinvestment, and the yield curve change your recommendation.</li></ol>
<p><a class="primary" href="chapters/project-appraisal.html?route=investment">Start the route →</a> <a href="#investment-takeaways">Jump to takeaways</a></p></section><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="project-appraisal" href="chapters/project-appraisal.html?route=investment">Is the project worth funding?</a><small>A project pays more next year than it costs today. Find the financing rate at which the decision reverses.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="risk-insurance" href="chapters/risk-insurance.html?route=investment">What is full insurance worth?</a><small>Compare the expected loss with the largest premium a household would pay to remove it.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="state-prices" href="chapters/state-prices.html?route=investment">Why is a recession payoff worth more?</a><small>Two claims have the same average payoff. Recover their prices by building portfolios that reproduce their payments.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="portfolio-choice" href="chapters/portfolio-choice.html?route=investment">How much should you put in each fund?</a><small>Vary the weights of two risky funds and find the allocation with the lowest volatility.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="market-risk" href="chapters/market-risk.html?route=investment">Which risks command a premium?</a><small>Two funds have the same volatility. Use their market exposures to judge whether the same forecast return is equally attractive for both.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="behavioral-finance" href="chapters/behavioral-finance.html?route=investment">Which holding would you sell?</a><small>Make a sale decision twice, then test whether a change in the purchase history justifies changing your order.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="long-run-valuation" href="chapters/long-run-valuation.html?route=investment">What growth rate belongs in terminal value?</a><small>Audit a perpetual-growth assumption by tracing productivity, market share, and the investment required to grow.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="yield-curves" href="chapters/yield-curves.html?route=investment">Which debt is exposed to a rate increase?</a><small>Reprice two repayment schedules under different yield curves and identify the cash the borrower must actually refinance.</small></li></ol><section class="route-takeaways" id="investment-takeaways" aria-labelledby="investment-takeaways-title">
<h3 id="investment-takeaways-title">Investment analysis takeaways</h3><ul><li>Match discounting to cash-flow timing and risk.</li><li>Evaluate an asset in the portfolio it will join. Correlation affects diversification, and beta is the market-risk measure in the CAPM example.</li><li>Stress the assumptions doing the most work, especially terminal growth, reinvestment, and the rates used for distant payments.</li></ul>
<h4>Put it together</h4><p>An analyst recommends a long-duration stock because new equipment lifts output next year and the stock looks cheap at a 5% terminal growth rate. How would you review it?</p><details><summary>Read a worked response</summary><p>Put the one-time productivity gain and the equipment cost into the dated cash flows. Test whether the business can sustain 5% growth and what it must reinvest to do so. Revalue at a higher discount rate and check how the stock changes portfolio risk before recommending an allocation.</p></details>
<p><a href="#investment-overview">Back to the overview</a></p></section></details><details class="map-route" id="credit" data-route-name="Credit and banking"><summary><span>Credit and banking</span><em>Which borrowers can repay, and which contracts give them a reason to do so?</em><small>7 lessons</small></summary><section class="route-brief" id="credit-overview" aria-labelledby="credit-overview-title"><h3 id="credit-overview-title">How this route fits together</h3>
<p>Imagine you are deciding whether to lend, on what terms, and what to monitor after closing. Work from the borrower’s choices to the bank’s cash needs. Keep a note of who bears the loss in each scenario and when payment is due.</p><ol><li><strong>Screen applicants.</strong> Ask who accepts the terms when borrowers know more than the lender.</li><li><strong>Design the contract.</strong> Check how repayment changes effort and how existing claims affect who wants to fund a new project.</li><li><strong>Monitor stress.</strong> Track equity, cash, interest coverage, and the amount that must be refinanced at maturity.</li></ol>
<p><a class="primary" href="chapters/adverse-selection.html?route=credit">Start the route →</a> <a href="#credit-takeaways">Jump to takeaways</a></p></section><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="adverse-selection" href="chapters/adverse-selection.html?route=credit">Who accepts the offer?</a><small>A buyer who raises an offer may change the quality of what comes to market. Work out which sellers accept and what their cars are worth.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="borrower-incentives" href="chapters/borrower-incentives.html?route=credit">How much can the lender safely promise itself?</a><small>Set a success repayment that finances a project while giving the borrower a reason to protect its cash flow.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="debt-equity" href="chapters/debt-equity.html?route=credit">Why would shareholders reject a valuable project?</a><small>Allocate a project’s cash flows among existing creditors and shareholders, then design funding terms both sides can accept.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="bank-liquidity" href="chapters/bank-liquidity.html?route=credit">Can the bank meet withdrawals?</a><small>Use a small balance sheet to find the withdrawal that exhausts equity and the larger withdrawal that exhausts cash.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="policy-transmission" href="chapters/policy-transmission.html?route=credit">Can the borrower cover its interest?</a><small>Trace a policy change through a floating-rate loan and distinguish a financing shock from a change in operating earnings.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="yield-curves" href="chapters/yield-curves.html?route=credit">Which debt is exposed to a rate increase?</a><small>Reprice two repayment schedules under different yield curves and identify the cash the borrower must actually refinance.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="foreign-currency-debt" href="chapters/foreign-currency-debt.html?route=credit">Can the importer survive a failed rollover?</a><small>Separate the dollar amount coming due from the amount the bank agrees to refinance.</small></li></ol><section class="route-takeaways" id="credit-takeaways" aria-labelledby="credit-takeaways-title">
<h3 id="credit-takeaways-title">Credit and banking takeaways</h3><ul><li>Loan terms change both who borrows and what a borrower does after signing.</li><li>Priority and collateral matter because they determine where cash goes in weak states.</li><li>Track solvency, liquidity, and covenant compliance separately. A borrower may still need cash on a particular date even if it has valuable assets.</li></ul>
<h4>Put it together</h4><p>A borrower offers a larger success repayment to secure renewal. Its loan resets next month and dollar principal is due before a major receipt. What should the credit memo check?</p><details><summary>Read a worked response</summary><p>Check whether the higher repayment leaves enough upside to induce effort. Recalculate coverage at the next reset and test cash available on the principal due date. If there is a gap, specify the amount and date to cover through committed renewal, earlier receipts, or another funding line.</p></details>
<p><a href="#credit-overview">Back to the overview</a></p></section></details><details class="map-route" id="treasury" data-route-name="Corporate treasury in Hong Kong"><summary><span>Corporate treasury in Hong Kong</span><em>How do supplier prices, currency exposure, and refinancing affect the cash budget?</em><small>7 lessons</small></summary><section class="route-brief" id="treasury-overview" aria-labelledby="treasury-overview-title"><h3 id="treasury-overview-title">How this route fits together</h3>
<p>Follow cash through a Hong Kong firm. A supplier quote, a project fee, a currency hedge, and a refinancing offer affect different dates and currencies. Start each lesson by writing down the amount, currency, and due date.</p><ol><li><strong>Start with the business decision.</strong> Compare unit margins at the capacity the firm can actually deliver and value projects after financing costs.</li><li><strong>Translate supplier terms into cash.</strong> Trace who bears a tariff and net receipts against bills due on the same date.</li><li><strong>Stress the funding plan.</strong> Distinguish changes in market value, the invoice exchange rate, interest expense, and principal due.</li></ol>
<p><a class="primary" href="chapters/costs-capacity.html?route=treasury">Start the route →</a> <a href="#treasury-takeaways">Jump to takeaways</a></p></section><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="costs-capacity" href="chapters/costs-capacity.html?route=treasury">Should the producer pass on a cost increase?</a><small>Use a price schedule, a capacity limit, and a rival’s expansion to decide how much of a higher unit cost customers will bear.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="project-appraisal" href="chapters/project-appraisal.html?route=treasury">Is the project worth funding?</a><small>A project pays more next year than it costs today. Find the financing rate at which the decision reverses.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="yield-curves" href="chapters/yield-curves.html?route=treasury">Which debt is exposed to a rate increase?</a><small>Reprice two repayment schedules under different yield curves and identify the cash the borrower must actually refinance.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="tariff-incidence" href="chapters/tariff-incidence.html?route=treasury">Who absorbs the tariff on a supplier invoice?</a><small>Trace a hypothetical duty through the exporter’s quote, the importer’s margin, and the customer’s price.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="currency-hedging" href="chapters/currency-hedging.html?route=treasury">How many US dollars should the importer hedge?</a><small>Match the size and settlement date of a hedge to the net dollar payment.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="hong-kong-exchange-rate" href="chapters/hong-kong-exchange-rate.html?route=treasury">What does the currency link protect?</a><small>Compare the exchange cost of a US-dollar invoice with the Hong Kong dollar interest bill needed to finance it.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="foreign-currency-debt" href="chapters/foreign-currency-debt.html?route=treasury">Can the importer survive a failed rollover?</a><small>Separate the dollar amount coming due from the amount the bank agrees to refinance.</small></li></ol><section class="route-takeaways" id="treasury-takeaways" aria-labelledby="treasury-takeaways-title">
<h3 id="treasury-takeaways-title">Corporate treasury in Hong Kong takeaways</h3><ul><li>A cost increase passes through sales, margins, and volumes. Check which constraint binds.</li><li>A hedge covers a specified amount and date. A late receipt can still create a need for bridge funding.</li><li>Market value and the cash needed for refinancing answer different questions. Put the principal and the funding spread on the maturity schedule.</li></ul>
<h4>Put it together</h4><p>An importer must pay US$1 million on day 90. A US$300,000 customer receipt may arrive one week late. What does a US$700,000 forward cover, and what should treasury arrange?</p><details><summary>Read a worked response</summary><p>The forward supplies US$700,000 on day 90. Arrange access to another US$300,000 until day 97 if the receipt is late. If it is cancelled, revise the net exposure because there is no receipt to repay a bridge. Check the reset date and cost of the HK-dollar borrowing separately.</p></details>
<p><a href="#treasury-overview">Back to the overview</a></p></section></details><details class="map-route" id="fintech" data-route-name="Markets and fintech"><summary><span>Markets and fintech</span><em>How do information, trading rules, and platform participation shape prices?</em><small>6 lessons</small></summary><section class="route-brief" id="fintech-overview" aria-labelledby="fintech-overview-title"><h3 id="fintech-overview-title">How this route fits together</h3>
<p>Begin with a trade, an application, or a payment and ask what happens behind it. The route follows the information revealed by orders and allocations, then shows how matching and settlement determine what users actually receive.</p><ol><li><strong>Read the signal.</strong> A price, an accepted offer, and a buy order tell you different things about what traders know.</li><li><strong>Check what gets allocated.</strong> Use IPO fills and available lending capacity to turn stated demand into expected outcomes.</li><li><strong>Follow settlement.</strong> Translate fees, timing, and redemption risk into usable cash.</li></ol>
<p><a class="primary" href="chapters/market-prices.html?route=fintech">Start the route →</a> <a href="#fintech-takeaways">Jump to takeaways</a></p></section><ol class="lesson-list"><li><a data-lesson="market-prices" href="chapters/market-prices.html?route=fintech">What can a price move tell us?</a><small>A share price rises after an earnings release. Decide which explanation you could defend in a morning note.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="adverse-selection" href="chapters/adverse-selection.html?route=fintech">Who accepts the offer?</a><small>A buyer who raises an offer may change the quality of what comes to market. Work out which sellers accept and what their cars are worth.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="dealer-pricing" href="chapters/dealer-pricing.html?route=fintech">Quote the next trade</a><small>A dealer sees a buy order but cannot see who placed it. Use the direction of trade to update the asset value and quote again.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="ipo-auctions" href="chapters/ipo-auctions.html?route=fintech">What is a share worth conditional on receiving it?</a><small>Compare a private-value auction with an IPO allocation in which the number of shares you receive conveys information.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="lending-platforms" href="chapters/lending-platforms.html?route=fintech">Which side of the lending platform needs a subsidy?</a><small>Use both sides of a lending market to find the constraint on funded loans.</small></li><li><a data-lesson="payments" href="chapters/payments.html?route=fintech">Which payment actually leaves more cash?</a><small>Evaluate fees, settlement delays, and redemption risk on the same date.</small></li></ol><section class="route-takeaways" id="fintech-takeaways" aria-labelledby="fintech-takeaways-title">
<h3 id="fintech-takeaways-title">Markets and fintech takeaways</h3><ul><li>Who accepts or trades can change the value of what you receive.</li><li>Applications, orders, and allocations measure different stages. Check the constraint before paying to grow one side of a platform.</li><li>Compare payments by when the funds are usable and what can reduce their value before settlement.</li></ul>
<h4>Put it together</h4><p>A lending platform reports more applications after a promotion and plans to offer merchants a lower-fee payment service that settles later. What would you measure before expanding either program?</p><details><summary>Read a worked response</summary><p>For lending, measure funded matches and contribution after screening and acquisition costs. If lenders are already the constraint, more applicants may add cost without funding more loans. For payments, compare settlement value after fees and redemption risk, and test whether the merchant can meet payroll before settlement.</p></details>
<p><a href="#fintech-overview">Back to the overview</a></p></section></details></div><section id="full-course" data-route-name="Full course"><h2>Full course</h2><section class="route-brief" id="full-course-overview" aria-labelledby="full-course-overview-title"><h3 id="full-course-overview-title">How the full course fits together</h3>
<p>Use this sequence to build the subject from the ground up. Each group introduces tools that the next group uses. You can start with Chapter 1 or open a topic to revisit a particular tool. The two evidence workshops and the Shenzhen memo bring the tools together.</p><ol><li><strong>Markets and firms · Chapters 1–4.</strong> Explain prices and quantities, then evaluate who benefits when resources are scarce.</li><li><strong>Risk and valuation · Chapters 5–10.</strong> Compare cash flows across time and states, then decide how much risk a portfolio can bear.</li><li><strong>Strategy and information · Chapters 11–16.</strong> Anticipate rivals’ responses, changes in effort, and who accepts a contract or trade.</li><li><strong>Banks and platforms · Chapters 17–20.</strong> Trace losses through balance sheets, measure spillovers, and follow payment through settlement.</li><li><strong>Macroeconomics and fixed income · Chapters 21–25.</strong> Separate real from nominal changes and trace shocks through earnings, loan rates, and bond values.</li><li><strong>International finance · Chapters 26–29.</strong> Translate trade, currency, and rollover shocks into the cash a firm needs by maturity.</li><li><strong>Evidence and capstone · Workshops 30–31.</strong> Build a comparable chart, design a test of the causal claim, and brief a credit committee.</li></ol>

Identify who can act, who knows what, and which constraint is binding.</li><li>Put cash flows on comparable dates and in comparable units. Stress the assumptions that could reverse your recommendation.</li><li>Separate what the data show from your explanation. Give the reader one piece of evidence that could change your conclusion.</li></ul>

How would you combine measurement, economic reasoning, and credit judgment in the memo?</p><details><summary>Read a worked response</summary><p>Report that exchange IPO counts fell from 187 to 133 between 2022 and 2023, while Shenzhen city resale prices were down 3.1% year on year in December 2023. Explain how fewer listings might affect local household wealth or employment, and consider tighter funding as a competing explanation. Compare neighborhoods with differing exposure to IPO employers and check their earlier trends. Treat the aggregate chart as context for the collateral review and specify what local transaction evidence would justify changing the haircut.</p></details>
